Network analysis of brain connectivity has been extensively researched, with functional connectivity being a key area of study. Building upon previous work, we propose a novel approach for modeling brain networks using total correlation theory. By applying this approach, we can capture the complex dependencies between brain regions, even in cases where relationships are not pairwise. Our method, based on entropy measures, allows for the exploration of multi-dimensional relationships within the brain, offering a more comprehensive understanding of brain connectivity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and real-world applications, showcasing its ability to capture the underlying structure of the brain and identify meaningful patterns in brain connectivity data.

The classical Segal-Bargmann transform's theory has been expanded to a space involving functions that take values in the Clifford algebra $\mathbb{G}_{n+1}$, which is linked to a Taylor transform. This extension has been explored within a Hilbert space context.

We are focusing on the Edwards-Anderson model on a finite graph, where we aim to establish a Gaussian field that represents the conditional measure given a specific set of spins on the model, with the values of the spins fixed at specific boundary spins. This field will be used to compute expectations of functions that depend only on the boundary spins, under the model's measure given specific boundary spins. We will compute these expectations efficiently using Monte Carlo sampling of the constructed Gaussian field.

This study examines the creation of a temporary, end-to-end network connection between ground-based and airborne sensors, enabling seamless data transfer. We develop a wireless communication system that allows an aerial node to establish contact with a ground sensor network, facilitating the secure and efficient transmission of sensor data. The proposed system leverages high-speed data transfer capabilities and secure authentication to ensure the safe transmission of data between the airborne node and ground sensor network.

The research into neutrinos using multiple techniques has entered a pivotal era, with the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE) poised to play a significant role. This experiment, utilizing a high-energy beam of neutrinos generated at Fermilab, will observe these particles over a long baseline distance of 4300 km, connecting the Fermilab site to the Sanford Underground Research Facility in South Dakota. DUNE's cutting-edge technology, incorporating a liquid argon time-projection chamber, will enable scientists to study a wide range of neutrino-related phenomena, including oscillation measurements, proton decay, and supernova neutrino detection. This review will delve into the DUNE project's scientific objectives, current status, and future prospects.

We've developed a novel method for improving top tagging by utilizing machine learning. The proposed model is built on 10 different tagging algorithms, which are combined to yield superior performance. The underlying assumption is that the best performance can be achieved by integrating the most valuable features from each individual tagger. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through successful application to both 2016 and 2017 LHC data, which yielded tagger efficiencies surpassing those of the CMS and ATLAS collaborations. Furthermore, we've utilized the Shapley value interpretation technique to elucidate the contribution of each component to the overall top-tagging efficiency.

This study establishes a precise definition for Virtual Organizations, defined as a coalition of autonomous entities working together to achieve a common goal, and introduces VO refinement as a means to transition between different coalitions of the same autonomous agents. We formalize these concepts using multi-agent systems and stochastic games theory and demonstrate that Virtual Organizations and refinement are achievable in an infinite game framework under limited information conditions.

A crucial component of model-free Reinforcement Learning, the policy optimization algorithm known as REINFORCE has seen its effectiveness limited by high variance in its gradient estimates. To address this issue, we have developed a new technique, called Variance Diminution Experience Replay (VDER), which mitigates the instability caused by high-variance gradient noise. By selectively sampling past experiences, VDER minimizes the adverse impact of high-variance states on the overall learning process. Our experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly reduces the instability of VDER compared to traditional REINFORCE, allowing it to learn more complex tasks, including games like Starcraft Multi-Agent Control, that were previously challenging for policy optimization.

A mathematical equation, known as the superbosonization equation and formulated by the author in 2005, connects two distinct types of integrals: one involving bosonic variables and another involving fermionic variables and their inverse. The equation's proof is presented here using a different approach based on the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation.

This research introduces a new framework, MoDeRNN, that enables the predictive learning of spatiotemporal data by considering distinct motion aspects. Building upon the success of ConvLSTM, our framework introduces a modular design that enables separate modeling of local motion, global motion, and long-term temporal dependencies. To capture the dynamic nature of spatiotemporal data, we also develop an adaptive module that adjusts the focus of feature extraction based on the data's changing patterns. To validate the effectiveness of MoDeRNN, we conduct experiments on three challenging datasets: the Challenging PETS2009 video dataset, the demanding DAVIS video dataset, and the complex COCO video dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that MoDeRNN achieves superior performance in tracking and object prediction tasks, while also providing valuable insights into the effectiveness of its unique design.

We introduce Josephine, a JavaScript library that leverages WebAssembly to efficiently handle the dynamic memory of the C++ RethinkDB store, ensuring the safe handling of its lifetime within the context of the browser's Node.js environment.

This research investigates the relationship between neutrino physics and particle colliders, specifically focusing on a particular type of decay known as neutrless double-beta decay at high-energy colliders like the Large Hadron Collider. The study considers the influence of heavy, neutral particles called sterile neutrinos and other particles that may exist, such as those with a different nature, on the decay process. The researchers found that certain combinations of heavy particles can significantly impact detection limits in experiments, even when these particles are within observable ranges at high-energy colliders. The study also explores the potential of using collider experiments to set limits on decay processes involving heavy, neutral particles, even when these processes are not yet directly detectable.

This paper introduces the first practical decoding algorithm for polar codes, effectively reducing the complex decoding problem to a more manageable subcode problem. The proposed algorithm, which builds on polar codes' properties, leverages their inherent structure to achieve this goal. The method, inspired by the polar code's inherent properties, offers a more efficient decoding alternative. The proposed algorithm's performance is demonstrated through simulation results, which show that it can achieve better results than standard BP and improved BP decoders, and comparable results to successive cancellation decoders.

When merging multiple images of the same area, each processed with different settings, combining their point spread functions leads to an inaccurate overall point spread function. We develop a method to determine which images should be included in the merge and their appropriate processing, ensuring the overall point spread function remains close to a standard form, such as the Moffat or modified Gaussian functions. This approach is demonstrated by applying it to the Perseus cluster, resulting in improved measurements of the brightness profiles of galaxies.

This paper utilizes the concept of a disclination field to investigate the fracture of a crystal, focusing on its interaction with the fracture surface and surrounding stress field. A fracture's shape and type of crack - stable or unstable - are determined by analyzing the disclination's behavior near the fracture tip. The paper also explores the impact of dislocations on the disclination's behavior, particularly when the dislocations are arranged in rows along the fracture surface. The study also examines the stress field surrounding the fracture, showing that it shares similarities with that of a dislocation. The results of the study are compared with existing theories of fracture, highlighting the relationship between the disclination model and other fracture theories.

We establish a probabilistic framework combining the Gaussian free field with Dirichlet boundary conditions in a unit disk, and multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution paths in the disk, whose dynamics are influenced by a random log-gas. This framework generates correlated Gaussian free fields and SLE paths that match an established theory by Dub\'ed\'eatin, Rhodes, and Vargas. Additionally, our framework allows for the generation of correlated GFFs and SLEs in the same disk, in addition to correlated GFFs and SLEs across different disks.
In this study, we derive prior estimates for the solution of the Navier-Stokes equations under external influences, using the maximum norm and periodic initial conditions.

A revolutionary quantum computer surpasses the capabilities of the most powerful classical computers, but the question remains on how to verify the results of the former, given the impossibility of the latter, to do so efficiently.
We introduce a novel verification method for quantum computation, which allows even the most basic classical computer to match quantum efficiency, with a constant factor overhead.
This verification method is based on the classical randomized model, and has a time complexity of O(T) for a quantum algorithm with S space and T steps, whereas the previous best known required O(T^2) steps.
Moreover, our verification method is the first to be correct in the unambiguous setting, and to work with the deterministic classical model, requiring O(T^3) steps.
Our results have significant implications for the fields of cryptography, complexity, and quantum computing, and pave the way for the development of unconditionally secure quantum services.

A significant concern in the IoT domain revolves around ensuring the integrity of data and network security. To address this, the adoption of blockchain technology has gained traction, particularly in developing robust and transparent data verification systems and safeguarding data against tampering. This paper focuses on a novel approach to integrating a blockchain framework with an IoT system, aiming to enhance data integrity and security through a combination of smart contracts and oracles. We demonstrate the practicality of this approach by applying it to the food supply chain, a sector plagued by counterfeiting and data manipulation issues. By embedding sensors in IoT-enabled packaging, real-time data can be collected and validated on the blockchain, thus facilitating the detection of fraudulent activities and the assurance of data integrity.

This research introduces a generative model that produces authentic cell forms by utilizing neural networks to depict intricate 3D shapes. We incorporate a biological component into the network's loss function, enabling the creation of cell-like structures inspired by natural models. To validate our approach, we generate new cell forms and conduct a detailed analysis of their morphological attributes, ultimately revealing the model's capacity to authentically represent and generate cells.

This study investigates the importance of document navigability for visually impaired individuals, focusing on a legal definition that necessitates accommodations for indented paragraphs and page layout features like headers and footers. We gather and analyze data from users who rely on assistive technology to consume digital documents. Our findings indicate that visually impaired individuals prioritize efficient content consumption over adherence to traditional document structure, with the ability to skip over unnecessary details being a critical factor in their user experience.

We introduce XLNet, a pre-trained language model that generalizes two widely used pretraining methods, namely masked language modeling and autoregressive language modeling. By combining these methods, XLNet capitalizes on both words' surrounding and forward predictive information. By removing the unidirectional limitation of autoregressive models, XLNet can learn more effectively from data. By counteracting the autoregressive bias, XLNet achieves better performance. By integrating the two methods, XLNet achieves state-of-the-art results on eight benchmark tasks across different information types and dataset complexities.

The detection of molecular signatures in the atmospheres of exoplanets through transit spectroscopy is a highly sought-after goal in the upcoming generation of space missions. However, signals from stellar activity can interfere with this process, and current research has primarily focused on its impact at high-resolution. Our study diverges from this by examining stellar activity effects at low-resolution, which is more significant in this spectral regime. We analyze the impact of active regions and rotating stars on transit spectra, and we find that even small features can distort the overall spectrum, resulting in pronounced absorption features. Moreover, we find that the effects of active regions on low-resolution spectra are more pronounced than at high-resolution. Our research also shows that high-resolution spectroscopy can effectively mitigate these stellar activity effects, and we find that the effects of activity on transmission spectra are reduced by a factor of 100 at high-resolution. Our findings suggest that future missions, which are primarily designed to operate at low-resolution, may need to incorporate high-resolution observations to accurately detect atmospheric signatures in exoplanets.

We construct a unique conformal metric on a non-compact Riemann surface with a specified number of "infinite distance" points and a unique conformal metric on a compact Riemann surface with "infinite distance" points. These metrics feature constant Gaussian curvature of -1 on their interiors and extend smoothly with non-negative Gaussian curvature on their boundaries. Our results build on the work of Schiffer and Stern, and are applicable in the context of the Teichmüller space and the study of hyperbolic 3-manifolds with geometrically finite extensions.

The unique ability of centipedes to traverse various terrains, including water surfaces, showcases their exceptional locomotion capabilities. However, the specific swimming techniques employed by these creatures remain largely unexplored. In this research, the swimming mechanics of the water strider centipede, Hygrotremius sp., are examined through high-speed video analysis and force measurements. The findings reveal that Hygrotremius sp.'s leg movements generate thrust and overcome drag to achieve propulsion, with the metatarsus and tarsi sections of the legs contributing to the process. The metatarsus propels the centipede forward, while the tarsi dampens the movement and maintains stability. The results indicate that the centipede's leg movements produce a combination of drag-based thrust and an inverted air bubble, similar to the swimming mechanics of insects. The findings also suggest that the centipedes' lightweight bodies and unique leg structures enable them to exploit the surface tension of water in a manner distinct from the larger insects.

This study presents a high-resolution simulation of a tsunami generated by a hypothetical asteroid impact in a coastal environment. We utilize a sophisticated numerical model, which employs a technique that adjusts the level of detail based on the tsunami's distance from the point of origin. By combining this model with a system that divides the computational domain into coarse and fine sections, we are able to simulate the initial wave and its propagation over various scales. The simulation reveals that the initial tsunami wave creates complex patterns of run-up and erosion along the surrounding coastline.

A new class of galaxies is being identified at high redshifts, exceeding $z=5$, which are characterized by their high star formation rates and low metallicities. These galaxies, known as IR-bright and O-dim, are difficult to study with traditional methods due to their obscured starlight. We analyzed data from the NIRCam and NIRSpec instruments on board the James Webb Space Telescope to investigate the properties of these galaxies. By examining their spectra and cross-correlating them with existing X-ray data, we found that the NIRSpec data is consistent with the galaxies' starlight, rather than being dominated by the hot gas typically seen in the X-ray band. This discovery has significant implications for understanding the evolution of the universe and its hot gas content.

In the realm of holographic field theory, researchers are exploring a new path in constructing geometrically-informed theories. This involves adapting established principles of supergravity to incorporate principles of general relativity, thereby facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between gravity and quantum field theory. The focus of this research lies in the Seven-Dimensional Gravity sector, where a novel coupling is introduced between a three-form field and a two-form field. The resulting action is then transformed through a dualization process, yielding a new formulation in terms of a two-form potential and a four-form potential. This novel formulation bears a striking resemblance to the well-known holographic coupling present in type IIB supergravity.

The critical density $\theta_{\rm c}$ for non-overlapping particle systems in a confined environment is a key concept in statistical physics. This paper focuses on the $\theta_{\rm c}$ of a system consisting of two types of particle-sized disks within a narrow, planar corridor. By examining alternating sequences of these disks, the study reveals that the critical density of this system is lower than that of a simpler, unrestricted version. The critical density of the confined system can be calculated using the largest eigenvalue of a specific transition matrix.

This research investigates how extreme ENSO events impact global precipitation patterns, focusing on extreme low and high precipitation events. Unlike most studies, which examine average precipitation changes, we use observational data to analyze the frequency of extreme precipitation events during specific periods. Our findings reveal that the amplitude of sea surface temperature anomalies during ENSO events influences the occurrence of extreme precipitation events globally. However, we also discovered that precipitation patterns associated with the amplitude of sea surface temperature anomalies differ from those associated with the timing of sea surface temperature anomalies. Our results indicate that the occurrence of extreme precipitation events during El Nino and La Nina events is influenced differently by the amplitude and flavor of sea surface temperature anomalies. Our research highlights the importance of considering both the amplitude and flavor of sea surface temperature anomalies when studying extreme precipitation events.

A new technique is developed to assess the non-uniform expansion rate of solid materials using photonic bandgap shifts in ceramic structures. The method enables assessment of material deformation at a microscopic level, which can be applied in scenarios such as solidification and additive manufacturing. The findings can be leveraged to investigate the inherent stress within 3D printed lattice structures and their mechanical properties.

This study examines single species with age structure, living in a polluted environment, and considers their avoidance behavior in response to toxic waste. We develop a nonlocal reaction-diffusion equation model, which accounts for age structure and age-dependent movement away from pollution. By applying the Laplace age-since-birth transformation, we derive an integrated reaction-diffusion equation and explore the existence and uniqueness of its solutions. Through analysis of unique stationary solutions, we investigate long-term model behavior and identify a critical threshold value that determines population survival or decline. Our findings indicate that a population can survive when pollution levels are below a certain threshold, and will eventually decline otherwise. Furthermore, our model's properties show that populations are more resilient to low pollution levels than to high pollution levels.

The concept of hypersequents, introduced by Avron, has been shown to be a versatile tool for proving the decidability of substructural logics that are too complex to prove using traditional sequent calculus. This paper delves into the characteristics of weakening and contraction in hypersequents, providing a systematic approach to translating sequent calculus to hypersequent calculus, thereby enabling the determination of the logical depth and decidability complexity for a broad range of hyperaccessible full structural superlogics.

Hierarchical taxonomy structures are ubiquitous across various domains, ranging from categorizing products to classifying languages, and are increasingly important in machine learning applications. Traditional methods for handling taxonomies often rely on pairwise relationships, which may not accurately capture inherent hierarchical connections. To address this limitation, research has focused on applying hyperbolic representation learning techniques, which are particularly suited to handling taxonomic data. However, existing methods primarily focus on learning optimal representations, without addressing the problem of predicting and representing new taxonomy categories. To bridge this gap, we introduce HyperExpan, a novel framework that enables efficient expansion of taxonomies using hyperbolic representation learning. By leveraging the unique properties of hyperbolic space, HyperExpan can accurately represent newly introduced taxonomy items, thereby enhancing search capabilities and maintaining the overall structure of the taxonomy. Our approach is evaluated on diverse datasets, including product categories and language classifications, demonstrating its effectiveness in predicting and representing new taxonomy items.

This study examines how external electric fields impact various non-covalent interactions between molecules. By applying up to 0.032 atomic units of field strength in two directions, researchers found that the polarizability of interacting species is significantly responsible for the field's influence. Specifically, the results demonstrate a notable increase in polarization under strong electric fields, with some cases showing up to a 20% enhancement of non-covalent interaction potential. Moreover, the study found that the direction of the field and the composition of molecular pairs significantly affect the interaction's response to the field, with certain configurations exhibiting a notable 20% increase in interaction under specific conditions.

A key component of Industry 4.0 is scheduling, which is critical for optimizing production processes. Traditional scheduling methods rely on deterministic or stochastic approaches, but these often fail to account for the complex, non-deterministic nature of modern industrial environments. This research introduces a novel method for handling complex uncertainty using a bivariate copula-based uncertainty set, which combines data-driven analysis with non-parametric estimation techniques. This method is then applied to the well-known Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (JSSP) to demonstrate its potential advantages over existing approaches. Our findings indicate that the proposed bivariate copula-based set effectively captures the uncertainty in job processing times, leading to improved scheduling outcomes compared to other uncertainty models.

This research introduces an innovative approach to evaluating the robustness of Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) over extended periods, focusing on the ability to recover from disruptions caused by deliberate attacks. We propose a novel method for modeling the robustness of CPS components over time using a temporal logic framework that accounts for both intentional disruptions and system recovery. By leveraging this approach, we can quantify the robustness of individual components within a CPS over an extended period, considering the dynamic nature of system interactions and impacts. Our method involves translating our logic framework into a mathematical expression over a system's behavior and computing its satisfaction value. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through several case studies, showcasing its ability to address various CPS scenarios and provide actionable insights for enhancing system resilience.

We introduce a novel approach to detect dark matter particles by utilizing a network of accelerometers. This method is particularly effective for particles with masses under 100 MeV. The strategy leverages existing accelerometer networks originally designed for geophysical research, enabling a cost-efficient search for dark matter. We develop a statistical analysis framework to analyze the data from these networks and establish constraints on the dark matter interaction cross-section. Our simulation results show that a network of just 100 accelerometers can set competitive limits by 2030, surpassing accelerator-based experiments.

Serrin and Galaktionov-Skrypnik developed innovative approximation techniques for the nonlinear diffusion equation with a gradient bound, which can be applied to the entire gradient family of problems. This paper utilizes Galaktionov-Skrypnik's method to derive a comparison principle for the nonlinear diffusion equation on complete manifolds. Consequently, under complete manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature, one can obtain explicit gradient estimates for the solution of the diffusion equation.

We conducted a thorough analysis of 24,114 obscure radio sources spanning frequencies from 1.4 to 8.6 GHz, found in the NRAO VLA Sky Survey. Utilizing Gaussian random field simulations and angular dimension stacking, we discovered that the distribution of angular dimension in the sources is non-uniform, with a concentration towards smaller dimensions. Furthermore, we found that the sources exhibit characteristics of both compact and faint radio sources, with a correlation between their size and flux density. Additionally, we discovered that the sources show a concentration towards smaller scales, with a correlation between their size and flux density. Additionally, we discovered that the sources exhibit characteristics of a fractal structure, with a correlation between their size and flux density.

This paper introduces a novel abstract model of hidden Markov systems, specifically for measuring information flow in systems. The characteristic function of an abstract hidden Markov model is utilized to quantify, in probabilistic terms, how likely it is for a system to behave in a certain way, given its initial state. This concept is then applied to information flow analysis in both deterministic and probabilistic systems. A significant outcome of this research is a generalization of the information flow index, which is defined as a mapping that relates a system's observable behavior to its internal state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the information flow index forms a measurable partition of the state space and derive an upper limit on the amount of information that can be extracted from a system's observable behavior.

By incorporating an exponential nonlocal weighting factor into the equipartition theorem, we develop a new statistical framework for analyzing complex systems with inherent system-wide connections. This approach is applied to various systems, including turbulent flows, ecosystems, and the stock market, all of which exhibit dynamic, self-organizing behavior. We demonstrate that this method effectively quantifies and measures the nonlocal characteristics of these complex systems, thereby providing a reliable measure of their global interconnectivity.

We introduce a parametric model for the behavior of high-energy particle collisions at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically at deep infrared momentum transfer values. This model, which is grounded in the principles of high-energy physics and the unitarity principle, is uniquely defined by just two parameters. It is capable of accurately reproducing the behavior of various theoretical frameworks, including QCD and the non-linear sigma model, and is consistent with the expected outcomes of effective field theories. The model's structure is derived from the fundamental properties of scattering amplitudes and their representation in the complex plane. It is shown that this amplitudes' behavior can be accurately described using the T-matrix representation of the S-matrix, which is characterized by its poles and branch cuts. The poles correspond to the exchange of particles, while the branch cuts correspond to the multi-particle thresholds. The model's coefficients are determined by the residues at these singularities, which are in turn related to the total cross sections of the scattering processes. The model's parameters are fitted to the total cross sections of the scattering processes, which are measured in experiments. The model's predictions for the differential cross sections are then compared to the results of Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data. The model's predictions are shown to be in excellent agreement with the results of the simulations and the experimental data.

A modified Planck distribution is derived by considering the Casimir effect's impact on blackbody radiation, taking into account the change in photon density of states due to the Cascer effect. The thermodynamic analysis of this modified distribution reveals that the Casimir effect has a negligible effect on macroscopic thermodynamic properties. The specific heat at constant volume, chemical osmotic pressure, and CH inequality are investigated in detail. The results show that the photon gas's behavior remains consistent with conventional blackbody radiation under the influence of the Casimir effect.

Protecting the location of a person over time is crucial for maintaining their privacy. This research focuses on developing a precise metric to evaluate how well different datasets can be pinpointed on various trajectories. To do this, we examine the likelihood of a person's location at any given time based on available information. This research introduces the concept of conditional priors, which allows us to calculate the probability of a person's location based on their past movements. To quantify how much information a dataset provides about its possible locations, we introduce the measure of directed information. This measure helps us understand how much a person's past movements reveal about their potential locations. By applying this measure, we can compare and assess the privacy of different datasets, especially those with different sizes. Our analysis also shows that smaller datasets tend to have lower levels of privacy, making them less predictable in terms of their future locations.

The 3D point cloud localization problem has been effectively addressed by the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) method, which approximates a point cloud with parametric distributions. However, representing the entire point cloud as a collection of NDT components is computationally intensive, making it unsuitable for real-time applications. To overcome this limitation, we propose NDT-Transformer, a novel approach that leverages the transformer architecture to efficiently process large-scale scenes and locate a robot's position within a fraction of a second. The method involves training a transformer to recognize patterns in NDT representations and generalize across different scales, resulting in robust and accurate localization. Experimental results demonstrate that NDT-Transformer achieves state-of-the-art performance on the KITTI benchmark, surpassing existing methods with a mean absolute error of 0.123 meters and 0.086 radians.

The relationships between resting-state brain regions, identified through functional magnetic resonance imaging, are commonly quantified using Pearson's correlation coefficient. However, its reliability and effectiveness have not been thoroughly evaluated. In this study, we investigated the properties of correlation coefficients by analyzing synthetic data and examining the impact of various factors on the correlation of true relationships. We discovered that (1) the reliability of the correlation increases with the duration of the data collection, (2) the correlation accurately predicts the strength of the relationships in the population, but is influenced by the magnitude of the relationship, (3) the correlation accurately predicts the direction of the relationships, but is impacted by the number of sites and the magnitude of the relationship, and (4) the correlation is more sensitive to the magnitude of the relationship than the number of sites. These findings suggest that the relationships between brain regions can be reliably measured and accurately predicted, but the correlation is influenced by the duration of the data collection and the magnitude of the relationship.

We investigate the relationship between the minimum number of bits required for an identifier and the total energy consumption in a beeping network where this identification is used to establish connectivity. We introduce a novel energy-efficient beeping protocol that achieves optimal O(log n) bit complexity with O(n^2) total energy consumption, surpassing the previous O(n^3) bound. Additionally, we prove a lower limit of Ω(n^2) total energy consumption for any optimal bit complexity naming scheme, regardless of its design.

This study introduces a novel encoding method called Relative Positional Encoding (RPE), which is adaptable to variable word lengths across different languages, and is suitable for processing code-mixed texts. We also suggest dividing input sequences into segments based on language boundaries and applying a position-relative encoding technique to each part. By integrating this encoding method with the pre-existing multilingual model, PASTOR, our experiments demonstrate that RPE significantly enhances the performance of the model in handling code-mixed languages, outperforming the standard Transformer positional encoding across multiple tasks, including classification and sequence labeling.

Using a combination of first-principles calculations and the Allen-Dynes modified Debye approximation, we investigated the impact of a van Hove singularity on the isotope effect exponent and critical temperature in H3S, a high-temperature superconductor. The exponent's value, which is linked to the isotope effect, is influenced by the density of states near the Fermi level, and its variation with pressure is attributed to the approach of a van Hove singularity near the Fermi level. The exponent's value, which is around 0.3 to 0.4 at pressures above 150 GPa, is in line with experimental results. The calculated exponent's value also suggests that the superconductivity in H3S is primarily mediated by phonons. The calculated critical temperatures, which range from 200 K to 220 K, are in line with experimental findings. This research introduces a novel method for creating spatial constraints based on the trajectories of dynamic objects, which can be applied to navigate robots in environments containing moving entities. These constraints, which can be integrated with existing motion planning algorithms, help a robot avoid collisions with dynamic objects. A new category of spatial constraints, which can prevent robots from colliding with objects of equal velocity, is also proposed. Furthermore, dynamic obstacle avoidance strategies for both static and dynamically generated spatial constraints are developed and demonstrated through simulations.

This research introduces a visual re-localization technique that utilizes learned texture descriptors to generate texture-based matching scores.  We demonstrate that these scores can be combined with 3D scene reconstructions to achieve more accurate localization.  To address the challenge of building comprehensive 3D maps, we propose using object detection to automatically identify key features in images, thereby streamlining the mapping process.  This allows the system to scale to environments with numerous distinct objects, such as those found in a typical home.  Our approach, which integrates texture learning and 3D object-based mapping, achieves precise localization accuracy, as supported by our comprehensive evaluation.

In the context of multi-user MIMO systems, we've developed an efficient algorithm to jointly optimize user selection and precoding. This algorithm leverages the group LASSO formulation, which can be reinterpreted as a joint user selection and precoding problem. To achieve this, we've devised a low-complexity algorithm that alternately performs user selection and precoding. Notably, our results show that this approach yields better performance than the maximum SINR-based method, and our simulation outcomes align with theoretical predictions.

For a tropical curve, the rational function semifield is proven to be generated by a finite set of rational function elements. Moreover, the coefficients in this generation are rational with non-negative tropical valuations.

This study examines the uniform convergence rate of the sample-based Q-function estimator to the true Q-function in finite Markov decision processes. We establish a lower bound condition on the transition matrix that prevents the Markov chain from becoming trapped in isolated subsets of the state space. Utilizing this assumption, we derive a uniform convergence bound for the empirical Q-function toward the true Q-function. We then apply this result to the exploration bonus based Q-learning algorithm to quantify its rate of uniform convergence to the optimal Q-function.

We've created a specific base for 3-row 3-particle braids, which is formed from compositions of a fundamental building block known as the Fox-Hatcher loop. In our research, we demonstrate that this base is formed by taking the braiding permutations associated with this loop and the three fundamental 3-particle generators, which are themselves created through the application of three distinct Artin generators. Furthermore, we calculate that a Vassiliev invariant of order three, denoted as v_3, assigns the value zero to the Fox-Hatcher loop when it is applied to any element within our base, except for the trivial base element, which serves as a key component in our proof that v_3 is equal to the p-Vierwinden invariant p_V.

Using the dynamical mean-field theory, our study investigates how electronic fluctuations impact the superconducting properties of LiFeAs, an iron-based superconductor. The research reveals that under certain conditions, specifically when the Hund's coupling is greater than 1.5 and electronic fluctuations are strong, the system exhibits a nematic phase at low temperatures. However, when comparing the results to experimental data, we find that LiFeAs does not show signs of this phase transition, suggesting that the system's superconducting properties are not influenced by nematic fluctuations. The current study's findings suggest that the system's superconducting properties are not influenced by the system's electronic fluctuations, and that the system's superconducting properties are not influenced by the system's electronic fluctuations, and that the system's superconducting properties are not influenced by the system's electronic fluctuations.

We investigate the alignment of the two Higgs doublet model under various conditions, taking into account the results from the LHC and the anticipated LHC Run 3 and HL-LH experiments. Our analysis considers two distinct scenarios: one where Higgs boson decay to photons is modified and another where it isn't. In these scenarios, the photon decay channel significantly impacts the two Higgs doublet model's parameter space. With the ongoing LHC experiments, this impact is further constrained. In contrast, the Higgs boson's mass difference with the standard model remains unaffected. Furthermore, the mass of the new neutral Higgs boson is constrained to be at least 510 GeV for a specific scenario and at least 340 GeV for another, under a 95% confidence level.

To create artificial systems capable of autonomous self-reproduction, self-organization, and adaptation, researchers are developing novel approaches to simulate the self-assembly of matter. Our work utilizes neuroevolution to design autonomous particle agents that can learn the rules of self-assembly. These agents, referred to as molecular learning agents or MLAs, learn self-assembly strategies by interacting with a simulated environment. Our research demonstrates successful self-assembly in multiple scenarios, including adhesion-based self-assembly, crystallization, and the formation of 2D and 3D crystal structures. Our findings suggest that self-assembly can be achieved without predefined rules by using artificial intelligence.

The anomaly-robust anomaly-robust insulators (RAI) phases in chiral gauge theories with multiple fermions are explored. These RAIs phases are found to be topological, non-trivial, and insulating, with the presence of topological order and emergent symmetries. The phases are robust against perturbations that preserve the gauge symmetry, with the number of distinct insulating phases for theories with n Weyl fermions being determined by the number of ways to partition n into sets of size 6 or more. The research also discusses the properties of fermion phases in the context of the spin charge separation and the properties of boson phases in the context of the Z_6 emergent symmetry.

We demonstrate that the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in three-dimensional space exhibit an essential ill-posedness in low-regularity Besov spaces, specifically in spaces denoted as $\dot{B}^{d-p}_{p, \infty}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ for $d \geq 2$ and $2 \leq p < \frac{2(d+1)}{3}$. This outcome stems from the proof of the norm's inability to be closed under the stationary Navier-Stokes semigroup, an application of which reveals the non-uniqueness of solutions for certain initial data.

We have developed a statistical mechanics framework to investigate the phenomenon of thermal squeezing in magnons within antiferromagnetic materials. A two-level antiferromagnetic unit cell is coupled to a heat bath, and we have introduced a classical nonlinearity that affects the system. We have also applied the method of linearizing a quantum Rabi model to calculate the magnon occupation numbers and their correlations. The results show that thermal squeezing can occur in magnons under specific conditions, and we have observed significant spectral shifts due to both non-linear interactions and thermal effects. The phenomenon of thermal squeezing is influenced by both the non-linear interaction and thermal bath temperature.

Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem, built on a linear code with repeated coordinates, offers two possible vulnerabilities to structural attacks. The first involves the public matrix having a low-rank component that can be exploited, while the second involves the private code having low weight components that can be used in a key recovery attack. To address these issues, we propose two modifications that use specific types of permutations and mappings to obscure the system's structure. Specifically, these modifications use derangements and non-linear functions to disguise the system, making it resistant to known attacks. However, we also present a new polynomial-time attack that takes advantage of the modifications, using a combination of linear equations and information sets to recover the secret key.

Language pre-training has greatly benefited from using large datasets and advanced architectures. However, limitations in our languages' resources hinder the effectiveness of pre-training models. To overcome this obstacle, we developed a method to incorporate supplementary information from a thesaurus into pre-training models. This improvement led to significant enhancements in our language's state-of-the-art pre-training model.

The study focuses on the mathematical properties of random complex structures, specifically the mass of a minimal network and the distribution of a diagram that captures the evolution of these complex systems over time. We establish that under certain conditions, the mass of this minimal network grows in a predictable manner as the size of the data set increases, and we also show that the distribution of a diagram that captures the evolution of these complex structures converges to a specific pattern. This specific pattern is generated by random complex structures, which can be thought of as a higher-dimensional version of a familiar model used in statistical analysis. Our results provide new insights into the behavior of these complex structures and have potential applications in a variety of fields, including physics, biology, and engineering.

In recent years, the Federated Learning (FL) framework has garnered significant interest for its ability to train machine learning models while preserving user data confidentiality. A growing trend in research has focused on exploring vulnerabilities in the federated learning process, particularly in the context of vertical federated learning (VFL), a setup where users' data resides on separate servers. A recently introduced attack, known as the membership inference attack (MIA), poses a significant threat to user privacy in both vertical and horizontal federated learning environments. A MIA attack seeks to identify specific data points that contributed to a model's training, effectively mimicking a non-participant with the data point in question. To address MIA vulnerabilities in the VFL framework, we introduce the first comprehensive study of this issue within this setting. Our investigation reveals that existing MIA attacks are largely ineffective in the VFL framework, prompting us to introduce novel attack methods that pose a significant threat to user privacy. Our experiments, conducted on real-world datasets, demonstrate that the proposed attacks can successfully identify data points with high accuracy, even when the attacker lacks access to a substantial portion of the global model, and when the model is relatively small.

Dark matter candidates include dark baryons, which can be created in $B$-meson decays, but these processes are complex and difficult to analyze. A novel method has been developed to calculate physical decay rates using light-cone series rules, which can also be used to model other important decay processes. To make this approach practical, mathematical formulas have been derived that describe key particle waveforms. These rules have been applied to two types of decays, which produce a dark proton, and calculations have been performed for their rates. The results show that one decay rate is significantly higher than the other, with a numerical value of approximately $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$, and this outcome has implications for the distribution of dark matter in the universe.

In the rapidly evolving landscape of urban environments, cities are increasingly vulnerable to socio-cyber-physical attacks that can disrupt critical infrastructure and cause significant harm. To effectively mitigate these threats, cities must invest in robust defense mechanisms, but limited resources necessitate strategic allocation. This study introduces an innovative framework for city defense, where cities can simulate attack scenarios and develop optimal resource distribution strategies to counter potential vulnerabilities. The framework incorporates a multi-agent attack model that considers diverse city characteristics and resource constraints, and employs reinforcement learning to identify the best defense configurations. Through comprehensive simulations, the effectiveness of the proposed defense strategy is demonstrated, offering valuable insights for cities to enhance their security resilience.

In the Hawking-Page transition, the thermodynamic equilibrium between small black holes and thermal radiation shifts to small black holes and confining gauge theories, and then to large black holes in anti-de Sitter space. Researchers have previously explored this transition within pure anti-de Sitter space, and now we have re-examined and reinterpreted the Hawking-Page transition when a confining box is present. In a simple model, we have analyzed how the system's behavior changes in response to variations in the box's size, and found that a critical size exists at which the system undergoes a phase shift in black hole behavior.

In the field of document ranking, labeled noise is a significant challenge. 
Existing approaches to mitigate labeled noise typically involve either discarding 
unreliable labels or down-weighting them, but these methods are not 
effective for large datasets. In contrast, our novel approach to information 
retrieval for labeled noise in document ranking utilizes bagging to create 
multiple subgroups, each with its own set of pseudo labels, and then trains 
ranking models for each subgroup. By aggregating the predictions from these 
models, we obtain final rankings that are resistant to labeled noise. 
Furthermore, we have developed a novel loss function that leverages subgroup 
rankings to improve the model's robustness to labeled noise. 
Our experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art 
approaches in robust document ranking and that our proposed loss function 
significantly enhances the model's resilience to labeled noise.

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in semi-supervised learning tasks, particularly for pseudo-labeling. However, the majority of these methods rely on the assumption that all generated pseudo-labels are reliable, which is often not the case in reality. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Informative Pseudo-Labeling with Pseudo-Tagging (IPL2P), which aims to enhance pseudo-labeling by incorporating a reliable subset of informative pseudo-labels. Unlike previous methods that focus solely on minimizing the loss function, IPL2P leverages the predictive confidence of the GNN to tag and select informative pseudo-labels. Furthermore, IPL2P employs a novel loss function that combines cross-entropy and entropy minimization to achieve this. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets show that IPL2P outperforms state-of-the-art methods in semi-supervised learning.

Betatron radiation holds potential for non-invasive diagnostics in plasma wakefield acceleration, particularly when using a helical electron plasma perturbation introduced by a plasma crystal in the AWAKE Run 2 experiment. This study provides a detailed simulation analysis of the betatron radiation emitted by an electron test bunch as it is accelerated by the plasma perturbation introduced via a laser in the AWAKE Run 2 setup. The simulations reveal that the emitted radiation exhibits distinct characteristics, including an elliptical electron bunch shape and specific emission patterns, which can be observed on an optical sensor. These simulation results align with experimental findings from AWAKE Run 2.

The widespread adoption of machine learning has led to a significant demand for privacy-preserving techniques, particularly in the processing of sensitive data. Among these, secure computation methods such as homomorphic encryption and secret sharing, as well as trusted execution environments, have been extensively studied. However, these methods are typically designed for data that is already securely shared, and not for data that is simply confidential. To address this issue, we have developed a novel framework for incorporating differential privacy into distributed machine learning tasks. Our approach utilizes a statistical aggregation method, the histogram-based aggregation, to facilitate secure data analysis. By combining this with a new differential privacy mechanism, we have been able to effectively protect sensitive data. Our proposed method has been successfully applied to the training of decision trees, achieving significant improvements in both accuracy and data protection. Our results demonstrate that, even with limited data protection budgets, our method can achieve high accuracy while still effectively safeguarding sensitive information.

We propose a new optimization approach to minimize the R\'enyi divergence between two probability distributions, incorporating a prior, with a focus on cases where one distribution contains noise. The problem is complex due to its non-convex and non-smooth nature, so we apply Tikhonov regularization to obtain a simplified, convex but non-smooth problem. The conditions for the resulting problem's convergence to a unique solution are identified and formulated in terms of probability distribution support and a kernel matrix. Building on this, we develop an algorithm based on Bregman proximal gradient descent, and prove its non-increasing convergence in terms of R\'enyi divergence. The algorithm's convergence rate is also analyzed, and it is demonstrated that it can achieve optimal rates in specific scenarios.

This research introduces a Bayesian method for selecting the most effective Chain Event Graph models using the Maximum A Posteriori approach. We adapt a model selection technique originally developed by Tutz et al. (2016) for Logistic Regression, incorporating a Bayesian information criterion and employing Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation to approximate the model's likelihood. Our simulation results indicate that the selected models perform well in terms of predictive accuracy.

This research introduces a novel dynamical system that strongly converges to the least norm solution of a constraint system governed by linear constraints. The system, which is linear constraints optimal path finding, is an extension of the system, linear constrained Hamiltonian dynamics, that was developed in \cite{CCL21}. By incorporating a damping term and a vanishing regularization parameter, the system's trajectories strongly converge to the least norm solution. When the damping term is time-dependent, the rate of convergence is determined by a balance between the damping and regularization parameters.

Our goal is to investigate how a simple robot mimics wall tracing in the presence of minor position and orientation inaccuracies. We've created a straightforward mathematical model that represents the robot's movement, and through numerical simulation, we've discovered that the robot exhibits complex behavior, including chaotic and wall-tracing patterns, which are influenced by a parameter. This research reveals that the understanding of these models is crucial for developing reliable autonomous systems.

We investigate the impact of impurities on the dynamic conductivity of kinetic energy driven superconductors in the normal state, employing the Boltzmann equation. Our analysis reveals that normal state microwave conductivity is significantly influenced by the scattering mechanism associated with impurities. When considering local impurities, our results indicate a peak in conductivity at low frequencies, whereas the conductivity curve for non-local impurities exhibits a peak at high frequencies. This discrepancy arises from the dynamic nature of kinetic energy driven superconductors near the Fermi surface. Notably, the magnitude of conductivity is substantially reduced when accounting for non-local impurities compared to their local counterparts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the microwave conductivity of kinetic energy driven superconductors is highly sensitive to impurity non-locality length, providing a means to distinguish between local and non-local impurities through experimental measurements.

This passage discusses the long-term evolution of planar curves with finite length, characterized by a geometric function known as $\cos\kappa_s$, where $\kappa_s$ represents the curvature at point $s$. It also explores the mathematical operator $\partial_{s}\cos\kappa_s$ and provides a comprehensive review of various results stemming from this operator, drawing connections to mean curvature flow and curvature flow.

Our ability to interpret and interact with our physical environment is a fundamental human trait, rooted in our capacity to understand and engage with our surroundings. Our knowledge of the natural world, including our capacity to grow and nurture plants, is a deeply ingrained aspect of our human identity. However, replicating these skills in artificial intelligence poses a significant challenge. Our research, GrowSpace, aims to teach robots the complex process of growing plants by providing guidance on plant care. This innovative system learns to recognize the state of a plant and recommends the most appropriate action to take, effectively adapting to the unique characteristics of different plants. By leveraging its knowledge base, GrowSpace enables the automation of plant care tasks, including watering, fertilizing, and pruning, ultimately transforming these activities into manageable routines.

The conformal welding SLE loop $CL(0)$ is redefined as the boundary of an SLE$(\frac{2}{3},\frac{2}{3})_0$-loop, and its properties in terms of chordal SLE$_3$ are examined. This involves analyzing Schramm's results on Brownian motion and zero-boundary harmonic functions, and exploring the relationship between Brownian motion and SLE curves. It is demonstrated that SLE$_3$ curves can be viewed as conformally invariant boundaries of quantum disks, and their length distribution can be derived from the time spent at the maximum by the Brownian motion on the boundaries of certain quantum disks.

A standardized set of tools comprising Python scripts and C++ libraries, known as IBNS, is designed to facilitate the creation and assessment of image biomarkers for medical imaging research. The toolset includes resources for image data normalization in accordance with the DICOM standard, enabling seamless integration with existing medical imaging workflows.

Furthermore, we found that the calculated real parts of the amplitudes are also consistent with experimental data, after accounting for the contributions of the high-spin nucleon and delta resonances. This research details the process of constructing a comprehensive database from raw data, specifically focusing on creating a database from images of faces. A detailed explanation of the methodology employed to establish the database is provided, including the extraction of faces from full images and the removal of faces that are poorly illuminated or not clearly visible. Additionally, the study outlines the removal of faces exhibiting signs of obstruction or damage. The study also covers the normalization of images to a standard size and the application of algorithms to align the eyes within each image. This work builds upon previous studies conducted by our research group on different databases, including the CMU-PIE and MORPH-II databases.

We explore the possibility of primordial black hole formation through the mechanism of a "curvaton," specifically when its field is coupled to a scalar field that exhibits "operational" behavior. The interaction between the curvaton and the scalar field generates primordial black holes as the scalar field's density fluctuations become amplified. The process of curvaton decay and subsequent particle creation leads to a universe dominated by these particles, potentially influencing dark energy.

This research introduces a latent variable model to analyze university course
data, which enables the simultaneous extraction of course attributes and
course progression pathways. The model's parameters are estimated using an
EM-type algorithm, and the methodology is applied to courses within an
engineering department. The outcomes of this study are compared to a
Markov-chain-based approach, and it is demonstrated that the proposed
methodology offers greater flexibility and more accurate pathway reconstructions.

Building upon the concept of cooperative driving, this study explores vehicle platoons as a form of decentralized leadership. The research considers multiple vehicle platoons where each leader is linked to its follower(s) through communication. The study models platoon dynamics as differential games, with each leader acting in a self-interested manner to optimize its performance. The study derives the optimal driving behavior for the platoons using feedback control, and demonstrates that this control strategy ensures stable connections between vehicles within the same platoon. The study further validates the proposed approach through numerical simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness in handling multiple vehicle platoons simultaneously.

The relationship between an explanatory variable and an outcome variable can be affected by another variable, known as an interaction effect, which is common in real-world scenarios. In the context of the widely used logistic regression model, we explore how to prevent main effects from being statistically linked to a specific outcome variable, given interaction terms and data. By identifying the conditions under which the model's parameters remain unchanged, our solution involves setting the coefficients of interaction terms to one minus the sum of their respective coefficients, which maintains the variable's overall influence on the outcome variable's probability, preserving the model's interpretability, and demonstrating its applicability through an example involving online ad click-through rates.

The proliferation of fake news on social media has led to growing interest in detecting news headlines that are not authentic.  This study proposes a novel approach to identifying automatically generated news headlines by modifying the BERT model.  The modified model, known as BERT-Headline, outperforms the baseline BERT model by achieving an accuracy of 0.966 compared to the baseline's 0.960.  This improvement is attributed to the incorporation of a news headline-specific vocabulary, which enhances the model's ability to identify automatically created headlines.  The BERT-Headline model's performance is validated using two news headline datasets.

We investigate the polycrystalline and amorphous forms of the chiral Heisenberg model in order to identify polycrystalline and amorphous realizations of the chiral spin liquid phase. By examining the chiral order parameter and the energy gap, we find that the polycrystalline state exhibits the chiral spin liquid phase at low temperatures, while the amorphous state displays it at both low and high temperatures. Additionally, we analyze the topological structure of these realizations by studying string excitations and observing that the polycrystalline amorphous states share the same topological characteristics.

Radio astronomy projects, such as ALMA and SKA, are set to revolutionize our understanding of the universe. These projects will generate massive amounts of data, consisting of $N$ up to $10^9$ data streams. Traditionally, processing this data required $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ computational resources, making it impractical for large datasets. To overcome this challenge, we've developed a series of new algorithms that can be executed in $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ time. These algorithms rely on exploiting correlations between data streams and their shared properties, allowing for efficient data processing. By using these new algorithms, we can significantly reduce the time required for data calibration, opening up the possibility of processing large datasets from future radio astronomy projects.

The primary goal of portfolio construction is to create a portfolio that meets specific objectives.  Previous research has focused on portfolio optimization, which often relies on the assumption that asset returns follow a normal distribution.  However, actual returns exhibit non-normal characteristics, and assuming they are normal can lead to inaccurate portfolio recommendations.  To address this issue, we propose a new approach that involves using an autoencoding conditional generative adversarial network to learn the true probability density function of market returns.  By training this model on historical data, we can generate synthetic samples that accurately represent the market's potential outcomes.  We then use these generated samples to create more effective portfolios.  Our approach has been tested and shows significant improvements over traditional methods that rely on historical means and covariance, particularly when incorporating non-linear constraints.

The gluon-to-quark polarized transition matrix element $A_{gq}(N)$ plays a crucial role in the evolution of polarized parton distribution functions and is particularly important for $N$ values greater than 1.  As a key quantity, $A_{gq}(N)$ receives its primary contribution from the $O(\alpha_s^4)$ term in the variable flavor number scheme, which has been partially addressed in previous works.  In this research, we present the complete calculation of the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ corrections to $A_{gq}(N)$, which were found to be numerically insignificant.  We also provide the corresponding $O(\alpha_s^2)$ corrections for completeness.

This study utilizes the 3-year, 0.3-300 GeV gamma-ray data from the Fermi-LAT to investigate the characteristics of 105 blazars located within 100 Mpc.  We employed the Bayesian neural network to classify these blazars into four categories: Flat Spectrum Radio Quasar (FSRQ), BL Lacertae objects with steep spectral characteristics (BL Lac), BL Lacerts with hard spectral characteristics (BLHc), and radio galaxies (RG).  We identified 11 new members of the FSRQ category and 14 new members of the BL Lac category.  We further examined the spectral properties of these blazars and discovered that the FSRQ category exhibits steeper spectra at lower energies and harder spectra at higher energies compared to the other categories.  We also found that the spectral break energy of FSRQs is significantly lower than that of the other categories.  Our results indicate that the spectral break energy of FSRQs is approximately 1.5 times that of the other categories.  Additionally, we discovered that the spectral break energy of FSRQs is approximately 1.5 times that of the other categories.

This study examines the challenges and difficulties that content creators face when producing social media content, focusing on accessibility issues. The research involved interviewing 15 social media content creators and documenting their experiences and frustrations. The findings highlight the lack of awareness about accessible content authoring as a significant barrier. The study also reveals that social media platforms are not designed to facilitate accessible content creation, and creators lack the necessary tools and support to do so. The research suggests that increased education and awareness, as well as the development of more accessible social media platforms, are essential to improve content creation and consumption.

We have developed a novel operation, known as the tensor merge, which combines two hypergraphs into a single hypergraph based on the interaction of their respective parameters. The resulting tensor merge hypergraph exhibits unique properties, including the relationship between its spectrum and the spectra of its component parts. Furthermore, our work demonstrates a connection between tensor merged hypergraphs and network data analysis. Specifically, it is shown that a particular type of network transformation, known as the k-clique network transformation, preserves the spectral information of the original network when it is tensor merged.

India currently lacks a space-based observatory capable of conducting visible and near-infrared astronomy, which significantly hinders its research capabilities in this area. To bridge this gap, the INSIST project is being developed as a groundbreaking space telescope that will operate across the visible and near-infrared spectrum, equipped with advanced imaging and spectroscopy capabilities. This cutting-edge facility will not only serve the scientific community in India but also make significant contributions to global astronomy research. By harnessing its capabilities, scientists will be able to explore distant galaxies, unravel the mysteries of star formation, and gain deeper insights into the composition of celestial objects, ultimately paving the way for a new era of astronomical discovery.

In the realm of Alzheimer's research, analyzing data from clinical trials is a critical task, particularly in trials where the primary endpoint is the rate of cognitive decline. A novel statistical method has been developed to detect time-varying effects on cognitive decline across various patient subgroups, such as different disease origins, genetic profiles, or demographic characteristics. This approach employs non-linear cubic splines to model cognitive decline patterns, allowing for the examination of complex interactions. To facilitate its application, an open-source R package has been created, providing a user-friendly interface for analyzing data and generating clear, interpretable visualizations. A case study involving the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative dataset demonstrates the utility of this method in identifying meaningful patterns.

We introduce a novel global approach to identify the most significant transition pathways between two specified states within dynamically complex systems characterized by multiple scales. This method surpasses traditional techniques by not being confined to analyzing pathways that originate from predefined sets of states. Instead, it focuses on the transition pathway that globally dominates across the entire state space. This pathway is exemplified in a two-scale system where the slower dynamics determine the transition pathway that globally connects two specified basins of attraction. Our algorithm, built upon an enhanced version of the action functional, enables us to identify this pathway globally, even in systems with multiple scales. This pathway is characterized by its higher probability of occurrence and is validated by numerical simulations. Our findings demonstrate that the transition pathway identified through this method aligns with existing theories and provides a framework for understanding transitions in complex systems.

This paper focuses on a parabolic variant of the complex Monge-Ampere equation defined within a bounded domain in n-dimensional complex space. The study establishes and compares two distinct $L^{\infty}$ estimates, corresponding to the elliptic and Gaussian types of the given equation.

We have developed a typed lambda-calculus that supercomes standard functions and includes the ability to perform equality checks across all types. The calculus is designed to maintain type safety and computational termination. It has been demonstrated that, despite these features, both type safety and computational termination can be enforced. Additionally, a fundamental loss of decidability for the type system is attributed to equality checks within the calculus. However, when restricted to the ability to perform equality checks for natural numbers, both the type system and computational termination become decidable.

This text presents a structural relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals specifically tailored for conditional measure flow applications. Conditional measure flow theory is a crucial component in the mathematical modeling of measures dependent on parameters within various fields including probability, physics, and beyond. In the context of this relationship, the conditional measure flow serves as the integrand of the Stratonovich integral, with its flow parameter acting as the flow variable. The explanation involves a method of integration by a change of variables, utilizing a transformation that is linear in the flow parameter's increment. This transformation is derived from the solutions of the adjoint equation corresponding to the generator of the flow. Notably, this relationship is presented as a generalized formula applicable to functional integrands as well.

A topological group's standard structure spaces were introduced by T. D. MacGregor in 1971, based on its discrete subgroup's open normality. A discrete subgroup is considered extensive if every open normal subgroup intersects with it. MacGregor established a one-to-one correspondence between an expansive discrete subgroup and specific group normal subgroups, leading to the definition of the maximal ideal space of its group algebra as a compactification. This compactification uniquely compactifies the topological group and has been further explored by various researchers, including Glazer, Kaniuth, MacGregor, and Stumpp. In this paper, MacGregor's original findings are generalized, and new examples of compactifications are constructed based on new properties of maximal ideals of group algebras.

This research introduces an innovative auxiliary task aimed at enhancing the cross-domain text-to-SQL capability by training models to grasp not just SQL queries, but also the underlying data and meaning behind them. The proposed auxiliary task encourages the model to capture the full semantic context of a query, rather than just its individual components. By integrating this task into the training process, the model's representation learning is significantly improved, leading to better SQL generation performance across various domains, as demonstrated through our experiments on two widely-used cross-domain datasets.

This study addresses the safe movement of robots within crowded areas by implementing an advanced navigation technique for both individual and groups of robots. The proposed method utilizes a predictive control framework to determine the optimal path for each robot, taking into account the likelihood of collisions and the uncertainty in sensor data. A data-driven method is developed to calculate the uncertainty in sensor data, which is then integrated into a predictive control strategy to ensure safe navigation. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulations involving multiple robots navigating a complex environment with unpredictable sensor data and varying levels of uncertainty.

We have conducted an analysis of the Andromeda XXV (A25) dwarf galaxy, examining its structure and composition. By utilizing data from the Gaia mission and Hubble Space Telescope, we determined the galaxy's properties and identified it as a dark matter-dominated system. Our analysis revealed that A25 is metal-poor and has a low central dark matter concentration. These findings are consistent with those of a baryonic 'core-collapse' galaxy, and we suggest that A25 is a member of the Milky Way satellite galaxy system. Our research also indicates that A25 is consistent with the abundance mismatch problem, which is a phenomenon observed in the Milky Way satellite galaxy system.

In the context of massive connectivity, we are tasked with developing non-orthogonal sequences that can be utilized in grant-free systems. The sequences' properties are specified by a binary vector, which outlines the desired auto-correlation and cross-correlation characteristics. We employ a two-stage genetic approach to tackle this challenge, where the first stage generates a suitable gene pool, and the second gene-editing stage applies targeted modifications to discover a sequence that closely matches the desired properties. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulation results, which show that the two-stage approach can successfully identify sequences that closely approximate the desired correlation profiles.

Several practical models for moist air thermodynamics are developed, comprising both simple and complex variants. Notably, simple models include the approximation methods proposed by Mason (1957, 1968), while complex models adhere to rigorous Pippard's approach. Pippard's approach is shown to be overly complex for real-world applications, whereas Mason's simple variant offers a more efficient alternative. By applying Pippard's method to the fundamental thermodynamic equation for moist air, multiple thermodynamic properties can be derived, including the total heat capacity, the specific heat of dry air, and the specific heat of water vapor. However, the method has limitations, such as failing to accurately account for the specific heat of liquid water and the specific heat of water vapor, resulting in inconsistencies with the established principles of thermodynamics. In contrast, the application of Mason's simple variant to thermodynamic equations yields results that are more accurate and reliable, particularly in the context of the specific heat of dry air, the specific heat of dry air, and the specific heat of dry air.

We establish a geometric approach to the external algebra of a matroid, which provides an efficient method for calculating the logarithm of the matroid polynomial, offering a streamlined version of the previously developed matroid polynomial by Casali and Sali.

The effectiveness of using neural networks for dialogue state tracking relies heavily on the quality of training data, which in turn relies on manually annotated data. However, end-to-end speech-dialogue systems that utilize automatically annotated data often fail to achieve comparable results. This is largely due to the discrepancies between automatically and manually annotated data, which stem from the uncertainties in speech recognition. To address this, we propose a novel approach that leverages ASR ambiguity to generate training data, which incorporates the confusion networks of speech recognition. By doing so, we can capture the speech-dialogue discrepancies and achieve better results in the task of tracking dialogue states.

Given a smooth projective curve and line bundles, this paper focuses on vector bundles with specific degrees when restricted to those line bundles. It provides explicit formulas for the count of such vector bundles that fit into certain extension vector diagrams and remains valid even in the context of curves defined over fields with positive characteristic.
